findings.proposition: Moderate weight loss improved insulin action before the measured adipose inflammatory markers declined.

sources.label: Magkos et al. (2016)
sources.directional_finding: At 5% loss insulin sensitivity improved without reduced measured systemic or subcutaneous inflammation; greater loss altered oxidative-stress, matrix and inflammatory pathways.
sources.study_exposure: Weight maintenance versus initial 5% diet-induced loss; later approximately 11% and 16% loss with abdominal subcutaneous biopsy and tracer/clamp measurements.
sources.study_finding: At 5% loss insulin sensitivity improved without reduced measured systemic or subcutaneous inflammation; greater loss altered oxidative-stress, matrix and inflammatory pathways.

assessment.study: Weight maintenance versus initial 5% diet-induced loss; later approximately 11% and 16% loss with abdominal subcutaneous biopsy and tracer/clamp measurements.
assessment.population: 40 adults with obesity and insulin resistance randomized; 33 completed the initial comparison and nine continued progressive loss.
assessment.result: At 5% loss insulin sensitivity improved without reduced measured systemic or subcutaneous inflammation; greater loss altered oxidative-stress, matrix and inflammatory pathways.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Actual losses 5.1%, 10.8% and 16.4%; no pooled inflammatory effect or universal threshold estimated.
assessment.evidence_summary: At 5% loss insulin sensitivity improved without reduced measured systemic or subcutaneous inflammation; greater loss altered oxidative-stress, matrix and inflammatory pathways.
assessment.limitations: Attrition and selected later subgroup; endpoint timing and depot specificity prevent universal mediation claims.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary full text: Methods, Results, Tables 1–4, tissue expression results and Discussion.

contextual.why_excluded: Does not measure a dietary intervention on adipose stress or establish a PM-to-Phenome causal relationship.

contextual.why_excluded: Does not measure a dietary intervention on adipose stress or establish a PM-to-Phenome causal relationship.

findings.proposition: EPA-rich supplementation lowered stimulated immune-cell IL-6 production in medical students.

sources.label: Kiecolt-Glaser et al. (2011)
sources.directional_finding: Stimulated IL-6 production was lower in the supplement group.
sources.study_exposure: Double-blind 12-week randomized comparison of 2.5 g/day omega-3 supplement (2085 mg EPA and 348 mg DHA) versus placebo.
sources.study_finding: Stimulated IL-6 production was lower in the supplement group.

assessment.study: Double-blind 12-week randomized comparison of 2.5 g/day omega-3 supplement (2085 mg EPA and 348 mg DHA) versus placebo.
assessment.result: Stimulated IL-6 production was lower in the supplement group.

findings.proposition: The green Mediterranean diet package reduced MRI-measured visceral fat more than the comparison diets in DIRECT-PLUS.
evidence_dependency: The 2022 VAT and 2024 proteome publications analyse DIRECT-PLUS (NCT03020186); count one intervention cohort, not two replications. PM8-F4 reuses the 2022 study for component attribution, not an independent food trial.

sources.label: Zelicha et al. (2022)
sources.study_exposure: 18-month healthy dietary guidance, Mediterranean or green-Mediterranean programme, all with physical activity; both MED groups received 28 g/day walnuts; green-MED added 3–4 cups/day green tea, 100 g/day frozen Mankai and reduced red/processed meat.

assessment.study: 18-month healthy dietary guidance, Mediterranean or green-Mediterranean programme, all with physical activity; both MED groups received 28 g/day walnuts; green-MED added 3–4 cups/day green tea, 100 g/day frozen Mankai and reduced red/processed meat.
assessment.population: 294 randomized adults with abdominal obesity/dyslipidaemia; 88% men; 79.3% had eligible follow-up MRI.
assessment.effect_magnitude: VAT change −14.1% green-MED, −6.0% MED, −4.2% guidance; weight-adjusted green-MED versus MED p=0.042, versus guidance p=0.07.
assessment.limitations: Open-label package, incomplete MRI follow-up and post-randomization adjustment; no isolated food attribution or adipose inflammatory mediation.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary full text: allocation, exposures, MRI, results and adjusted comparisons; funding includes California Walnuts Commission.

sources.label: Zelicha et al. (2024)
sources.directional_finding: MED diets changed inflammation-related circulating proteins; green-MED showed more pronounced changes, with protein-cluster changes correlated with VAT reduction.
sources.study_exposure: Olink circulating-protein panels across the dietary intervention.
sources.study_finding: MED diets changed inflammation-related circulating proteins; green-MED showed more pronounced changes, with protein-cluster changes correlated with VAT reduction.

assessment.study: Olink circulating-protein panels across the dietary intervention.
assessment.population: DIRECT-PLUS participants: the same randomized cohort as the 2022 VAT report.
assessment.result: MED diets changed inflammation-related circulating proteins; green-MED showed more pronounced changes, with protein-cluster changes correlated with VAT reduction.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Reported adjusted p<0.05 for selected protein changes; no tissue-specific mediated effect quantified.
assessment.evidence_summary: MED diets changed inflammation-related circulating proteins; green-MED showed more pronounced changes, with protein-cluster changes correlated with VAT reduction.
assessment.limitations: Secondary proteomics, multiplicity and same-cohort dependency; circulating proteins do not establish adipose origin.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary abstract and indexed study results; full methods not independently recovered.

contextual.label: Willmann et al. (2019)
contextual.why_relevant: A separate six-month randomized dietary study compared reduced red meat and increased fibre within calorie restriction; visceral fat fell in all groups.
contextual.why_excluded: No additional cardiometabolic advantage of the food changes was established in that context; it does not isolate which green-MED component explains its package result.

contextual.label: Park et al. (2014)
contextual.why_relevant: A different pomegranate-vinegar formulation showed a preliminary CT-measured visceral-fat signal in overweight women.
contextual.why_excluded: Publisher-indexed abstract/result only was recovered; this is a vinegar-plus-extract formulation, not pomegranate fruit or a DIRECT-PLUS intervention. Independent efficacy and formulation details remain unresolved.

findings.proposition: The green-MED trial identifies walnuts as a food candidate, but does not isolate a walnut-specific effect on visceral fat.
evidence_dependency: DIRECT-PLUS component associations reuse PM8-F3 evidence; Njike and Dong are separate trials, but test different exposures.

contextual.why_relevant: Walnuts were supplied to both MED groups, and intake was associated with VAT loss.
contextual.why_excluded: The food association is not an independently randomized walnut effect; the package result is assessed in PM8-F3.

sources.study_finding: Adipose macrophages and MCP-1 decreased; capillaries increased; insulin sensitivity did not change.

sources.label: Fisk et al. (2022)
sources.directional_finding: Inflammatory transcriptome and oxylipin responses were more limited in participants with obesity.
sources.study_exposure: 12-week double-blind fish-oil concentrate (1.1 g EPA + 0.8 g DHA/day) versus corn oil with subcutaneous biopsies.
sources.study_finding: Inflammatory transcriptome and oxylipin responses were more limited in participants with obesity.

assessment.study: 12-week double-blind fish-oil concentrate (1.1 g EPA + 0.8 g DHA/day) versus corn oil with subcutaneous biopsies.

assessment.result: Inflammatory transcriptome and oxylipin responses were more limited in participants with obesity.

sources.label: Hames et al. (2017)
sources.directional_finding: EPA/DHA incorporation increased, without improved measured adipose inflammation or insulin regulation of lipolysis.
sources.study_exposure: Six-month randomized double-blind omega-3 formulation versus oleate placebo.
sources.study_finding: No measured tissue benefit despite increased EPA/DHA content.

assessment.study: Six-month double-blind placebo-controlled trial; 3.9 g/day EPA+DHA (4.2 g total omega-3) versus 4.2 g/day oleate.
assessment.population: Insulin-resistant adults with overweight or obesity; 12 supplement and nine placebo completers in the adipose substudy.
assessment.result: Adipose EPA/DHA increased, but macrophage content, crown-like structures, senescent cells and insulin regulation of lipolysis did not improve.
assessment.effect_magnitude: CD68 macrophages 31 to 33 per 100 adipocytes with omega-3 versus 33 to 31 with placebo; interaction p=0.25; lipolysis suppression interaction p=0.11.
assessment.evidence_summary: Tissue delivery was demonstrated without the expected inflammatory or lipolytic benefit.
assessment.limitations: Small completer substudy, baseline phenotype differences and subcutaneous-only sampling; not proof of no effect in every metabolic context.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary full-text Methods, Results, Tables 1–2 and Discussion.

findings.proposition: A simple claim that more magnesium reduces adipose stress is not established by the assessed evidence.

sources.label: Kurstjens et al. (2018)
sources.directional_finding: Low magnesium reduced high-fat-induced obesity and altered adipose lipolysis, while blood lipids remained high.
sources.study_exposure: 17-week low- versus normal-magnesium diets crossed with low- or high-fat feeding.
sources.study_finding: Low magnesium reduced high-fat-induced obesity and altered adipose lipolysis, while blood lipids remained high.

assessment.study: 17-week low- versus normal-magnesium diets crossed with low- or high-fat feeding.
assessment.population: Male mice, approximately 12 per diet group, plus a replication experiment.
assessment.result: Low magnesium reduced high-fat-induced obesity and altered adipose lipolysis, while blood lipids remained high.
assessment.effect_magnitude: High-fat group body weights approximately 47.0 versus 38.6 g, normal versus low magnesium; p<0.05.
assessment.evidence_summary: Low magnesium reduced high-fat-induced obesity and altered adipose lipolysis, while blood lipids remained high.

findings.proposition: Severe sleep restriction increased visceral fat during a controlled experiment with freely available food.

findings.proposition: Time-restricted eating showed exploratory adipose pathway changes in TREAD, but another trial found no extra visceral-fat reduction over Mediterranean-diet education.

sources.label: Wilkinson et al. (2026)
sources.directional_finding: Weight loss favoured TRE; inflammatory gene-set signals decreased in the selected biopsy subgroup.
sources.study_exposure: 12-week 10-hour personalized eating window plus dietary counselling versus counselling; exploratory subcutaneous RNA-seq in seven greatest TRE weight losers and six matched controls.
sources.study_finding: Weight loss favoured TRE; inflammatory gene-set signals decreased in the selected biopsy subgroup.

assessment.study: 12-week 10-hour personalized eating window plus dietary counselling versus counselling; exploratory subcutaneous RNA-seq in seven greatest TRE weight losers and six matched controls.
assessment.population: 61 adults with obesity without diabetes; 52 completed; baseline eating window at least 14 hours.
assessment.result: Weight loss favoured TRE; inflammatory gene-set signals decreased in the selected biopsy subgroup.
assessment.effect_magnitude: Weight difference −2.91 kg (95% CI −4.21 to −1.60); no individual transcript significant at FDR<0.05.
assessment.evidence_summary: Weight loss favoured TRE; inflammatory gene-set signals decreased in the selected biopsy subgroup.
assessment.limitations: Primary endpoint changed after last participant visit but before analysis; selected small tissue subgroup confounds timing with weight-loss response.
assessment.retrieval_scope: Primary full text including endpoint amendment, RNA-seq selection, FDR and results.
